newsitem.title: MEXICO: Super refineries hail dawn of return of raw sugar.
newsitem.headline: Super refineries hail dawn of return of raw sugar.

text.p: Planned new super sugar refineries around the world will lead to countries substituting traditional white sugar imports with lower quality grades, marking the beginning of a resurgence of demand for raws, experts said here.
Peter Hulme, former director of trading with Tate & Lyle and now with trade house, Sucden, told the F.O. Licht World Sugar and Sweeteners Conference that demand for low grade sugars is going grow.

"Except in the case of Taiwan, new refineries will replace white sugar imports with raws," Hulme said, adding that the principal market for resulting refined product will not be domestic consumption, but the export market.

Hulme noted that refineries had recently started production, or planned to begin this year, in Dubai (700,000 tonnes capacity), Mackay, Australia (350,000 tonnes), Indonesia (150,000 tonnes) Saudi Arabia (500,000 tonnes) and Taiwan (350,000 tonnes).
Also he said other refineries could be developed in Egypt (350,000 tonnes), Oman (150,000 tonnes) and others in Saudi Arabia (150,000 tonnes) and Indonesia (300,000 tonnes).

Hulme said the demand for low grade sugars had already started to show a steep rise. Including bagged raws, he said estimated low grades exports/imports will climb to 1.43 million tonnes this year from 480,000 tonnes in 1990.
Brazil's exports were expected to jump to 800,000 tonnes of low grades this year from 180,000 in 1990, Hulme said, adding that other countries were following suit.

Guatemala's low grade exports could hit 200,000 tonnes this year from 90,000 tonnes in 1990, Colombia 170,000 tonnes from 50,000, Thailand 200,000 tonnes from 50,000 tonnes, and other exporters 100,000 from 40,000.

Hulme said expectations were for those low grades to go to Sri Lanka (350,000 tonnes this year from 60,000 in 1990), East Africa (120,000 from 25,000), North Africa (100,000 from 20,000), West Africa (90,000 from 70,000), Egypt (80,000 from 220,000), with other importers taking the lion's share (690,000 from 85,000).

Tony Hannah, head of economics and statistics for the International Sugar Organisation (ISO), agreed that the construction of new super refineries in the Middle East might slow the growth of direct white sugar in the future and mark the beginning of a resurgence for raws.

Hannah said since 1993 demand for raw sugar has been good, partly due to the gap left by Cuba's decline in output and partly due to buoyant demand from Pacific Rim nations, notably Korea and Malaysia and latterly China and the Philippines, also after dips in output.

Brazil's surge on the international market, Hannah said, also had pricing implications, a reduction of the homogeneity of the market, because its exports have largely been in the form of crystal whites.
"These were sold at a discount to the standard white price and at the same time as very high pol raws at a premium to the standard raw price," Hannah said.
